captions.text: In the Chicago Fire demonstration department, we will compare Engine
51, Truck 81 and Reserve Engine 51.
These are fictional training resources.
Before opening a call, inspect each unit's type, station
assignment and current status.
A nearby unit in maintenance is different from an available unit.
Check that station coordinates are correct and that crews have
usable current assignments.
This preparation makes the nearest list an operational comparison instead of
a collection of unexplained distances.

Seven internal cuts use genuine one-second export anchors; no interpolated word times. Pre/postcrew and near/far states preserve the reviewed correspondence. No hidden/offscreen control promoted to visible.

captions.text: Open New Call and enter a training
name and nature.
Choose the intended type and priority, then
place a pin at the exercise location.
You can enter latitude and longitude and use Set Pin On Map, or use the location
tools your department makes visible.
Confirm the pin represents the incident rather than a station or destination.
Without a usable incident location, Resgrid cannot compare response distances.
Wait for the lists to finish refreshing after the point changes.

captions.text: Scroll to the unit dispatch lists.
The Units tab compares the units you may dispatch.
The Firehouse 51 tab shows our station resources.
This training department has all six units assigned to that station.
Read the current status alongside ETA and position.
Nearest badges identify the first available resources with measurable
distance in the ranked result.
They do not certify equipment readiness or crew capability.
Compare the named unit and its situation before ticking a recipient, even when
it carries the first nearest badge.

captions.text: The response comparison can include turnout as well as travel.
In Call and Dispatch Settings, set In-quarters turnout to 120 seconds for
this exercise, save, and
reopen the page.
Mobile turnout stays at zero.
Return to New Call and set the training pin again.
The unit rows now show an estimated two-minute response
including 120 seconds of turnout.
Here the origin is the station; this does not establish the
unit's physical location.
The distance measures separation from the incident.
An estimated time uses an approximation, while a provider-derived drive time
depends on the positions and route information available at that moment.

captions.text: Inspect Shift Coverage and Role Mix as well as response time.
Initially, our unit rows show No crew assigned.
Open Units, then Unit Staffing.
In this exercise, choose Christopher Herrmann for Engine 51's Officer or Team
Lead seat, save, and
reopen the page.
Engine 51 now says Fully Staffed because its one configured seat is filled.
That is not proof of a complete operational engine crew.
Define the seats and qualification requirements
your department actually needs.
Return to New Call and refresh the incident comparison.
Read the resulting crew and role mix rather than inferring them
from group membership, a vehicle's seats or its nearest badge.

captions.text: Click Station location for Engine 51.
The position panel compares its response origin with the call.
Here Resgrid uses the station origin.
That can happen for an In Quarters unit or when no usable GPS fix
is available; it does not confirm the unit's physical whereabouts.
Check the displayed source and any stale warning.
If a location is hidden from you, distance and ETA can also be withheld.
Do not fill that gap by assuming the unit is somewhere else on the map.

captions.text: Open Personnel and inspect the same response context for Christopher
Herrmann, our fictional officer.
Personnel have their own status and staffing information.
The positions in this exercise are simulated training fixes.
Read any stale label before relying on an estimate.
A person can be close to the incident without being available
for assignment, and an available person may have no usable position.
A unit assignment gives useful crew context, but it does not establish that
this person shares the unit's position.
Read the actual row rather than transferring a unit's ranking to
every crew member or assuming a role name proves current qualification.

scenes.title: Understand areas and scope

captions.text: Open Call and Dispatch Settings and review Group-Scoped Dispatch.
Response area boundaries describe which area contains an incident.
The Group Boundary editor under Stations and Groups is where those areas are drawn.
Our New Call comparison reports that the incident is not inside any group boundary.

captions.text: We will inspect the controls without saving a boundary.
Dispatch scope controls the candidates used for nearest comparisons.
These are separate settings.
This demonstration uses a department administrator with department-wide scope.
A unit can remain in the dispatch list without a nearest comparison,
so a missing estimate does not establish that the unit is unavailable.
When a comparison is missing, check the permitted scope, current status,
and usable position before deciding what resources are available.
We will return to New Call without changing permissions.

scenes.title: Move the pin and compare again

captions.text: Move the incident pin to a second training location and wait for
the refreshed response values.
Compare the same named units and personnel before and after the move.
Engine 51's distance changes from less than a tenth of a kilometer to
kilometers, while its estimate rises from two to 195 minutes.

captions.text: These are straight-line estimates, not a routed drive time.
A change in distance or turnout-adjusted time may change the order.
Check that the labels and pin still describe the intended exercise.
The system can retain the view you manually chose, so use the visible
coordinates and final list values as evidence instead of expecting every
refresh to zoom the map automatically.
In this station-based example, several units share an origin, so
their distances can change together without changing their order.

scenes.title: Make and verify the dispatch decision

captions.text: Return the incident pin to the original near training location
and wait for the values to refresh.
Select the resources that fit the exercise.
Here we choose Christopher Herrmann, the first nearby officer, and
Engine 51.
Engine 51 is third in the overall list, but it is the available engine;
the reserve engine is out of service.
Check that the unit selection agrees across its station and Units tabs.
If a run card also suggests resources, inspect that panel and
the final checkboxes together.
Ranking does not send anyone by itself.
Before saving, review the call, recipients and notification arrangements.
After the training save, open the resulting call, 26-4 in this
example, and its Dispatched tab.
Check Engine 51 and Christopher Herrmann against the intended recipients.
This proves the saved assignment; it does not establish that
a device received an alert.
Confirm member receipt separately.
Finish by closing only the training call with Send Notification
off, and
keep its history.
Keep the location source, freshness and estimated-time limits in
your decision, even when the first-ranked choice appears obvious.
The same review helps a mobile crisis team choose an available
clinician, a search and rescue team find a nearby qualified member, or a
security supervisor compare patrols.
Wildland contractors and industrial teams should also compare crew capability
and access to the incident before choosing the first-ranked resource.
